name: Executive order of September 12, 1872 setting apart the Malheur Reservation (the reservation itself)
nations: Burns Paiute Tribe (Wadatika band of Northern Paiute)
Snake or Paiute bands of southeastern Oregon who were parties to the unratified treaty of December 10, 1868
promises: The President set apart the Malheur reservation, from the mouth of the North Fork of the Malheur River up to Castle Rock, to Strawberry Butte, to Soda Spring, down the Silvies River to Malheur Lake, east to the South Fork and down it to the start; Royce says this embraces his areas 638 and 646.

breaches.what: Reciting its amended order of February 4, 1957, the Indian Claims Commission held that the Snake or Paiute bands who were parties to the unratified treaty of December 10, 1868 were deprived of their original Indian title to the former Malheur Reservation lands in January 1879 without any compensation, valued them at $579,722.00, and awarded that sum less offsets.

landTaken: Royce records that portions of the original reserve were relinquished by executive orders of September 13, 1882 and May 21, 1883. The Commission dated the taking to January 1879.
compensation: Award of $579,722.00 less offsets (1959 interlocutory order). No later payment was traced.

nationVoice.summary: The tribe writes that an executive order reservation of 1.8 million acres was set aside for its people but was short-lived, that survivors were marched to Fort Simcoe and Fort Vancouver, and that in their absence the reservation was returned to the public domain.

openQuestions: Possible duplicate: cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshoni-snake records the same executive order of September 12, 1872. That record maps Royce area 537 (the country withdrawn in 1871 and restored by this order); this record maps areas 638 and 646, the reservation itself. Same event, different polygons, so the same finding is used. Jordan may want the two merged or labelled "reservation" and "land restored".

treaties.json error: presentDayTribes is empty for this record; the Burns Paiute Tribe should be listed. It also links a statute file (638c.pdf) for what Royce lists as an executive order; the University of Georgia files did not load.
The 1956 Commission opinion (id 513) and the Burns Paiute page were taken from the parallel record and not re-read in this pass; the 1959 order (id 32) was re-read.

Audit 2026-11-08: the two Malheur records agree on the finding (January 1879 taking, $579,722.00 less offsets, parties to the unratified treaty of December 10, 1868), re-read in OSU id 32. This record maps the reservation itself (Royce 638 and 646), which the finding covers: the Commission's land is the reservation as defined on January 28, 1876, which Royce says took in all of the 1872 reserve. cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshoni-snake maps area 537, the country restored to the public domain in 1872, which the Docket 17 finding does not cover. Lead on the final award: a Commission order of May 31, 1960 on attorney fees (OSU id 33, 8 Ind. Cl. Comm. 512) refers to an award to the petitioners made in December; the figure (beginning $567,0) and the year are unreadable in the scan, so no final figure is recorded.

plain.promised: Not a treaty: an executive order. In 1872 the President set apart the Malheur Reservation in southeastern Oregon for the Paiute and Snake bands.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found the bands were deprived of the reservation lands in January 1879 without any compensation. Parts were returned to the public domain in 1882 and 1883.
plain.today: The Commission awarded $579,722.00 less offsets in 1959; no later payment was traced. The Burns Paiute Tribe says its people were marched away and the reservation given up in their absence.
